section.heading: 7.8. Improper Integrals
section.paragraph: In defining a definite integral $${\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)}}dx$$ we dealt with a function $$f$$ defined on a finite interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ and we assumed that $$f$$ does not have an infinite discontinuity (see Section 5.2). In this section we extend the concept of a definite integral to the case where the interval is infinite and also to the case where $$f$$ has an infinite discontinuity in $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ . In either case the integral is called an improper integral. One of the most important applications of this idea, probability distributions, will be studied in Section 8.5.
section.heading: Type 1: Infinite Intervals
section.paragraph: Consider the unbounded region $$S$$ that lies under the curve $$y = 1 \slash x^{2}$$ , above the $$x$$ -axis, and to the right of the line $$x = 1$$ . You might think that, since $$S$$ is infinite in extent, its area must be infinite, but let’s take a closer look. The area of the part of $$S$$ that lies to the left of the line $$x = t$$ (shaded in Figure 1) is
$$A(t) = {\int_{1}^{t}\frac{1}{x^{2}}}dx = - \left. \frac{1}{x} \right\rbrack_{1}^{t} = 1 - \frac{1}{t}$$

image.alt: Details A curve y=1/x^2 is graphed on the first quadrant of an x y coordinate plane. The curve starts by being parallel to the x-axis and gradually increases. The curve then rises at the point (1, 0) in which x=1 and goes up to the point where the curve is parallel to the y-axis. The points (1, 0) and (t, 0) are connected with the curve. The area= 1 negative 1/t is shaded.

section.paragraph: Notice that $$A(t) < 1$$ no matter how large $$t$$ is chosen. We also observe that
$$\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow\infty}A(t) = \lim\limits_{t\rightarrow\infty}\left( {1 - \frac{1}{t}} \right) = 1$$
The area of the shaded region approaches $$1$$ as $$\left. t\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ (see Figure 2), so we say that the area of the infinite region $$S$$ is equal to $$1$$ and we write
$${\int_{1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{x^{2}}}dx = \lim\limits_{t\rightarrow\infty}{\int_{1}^{t}\frac{1}{x^{2}}}dx = 1$$

section.paragraph: Using this example as a guide, we define the integral of $$f$$ (not necessarily a positive function) over an infinite interval as the limit of integrals over finite intervals.

note.source_type: Definition of an Improper Integral of Type 1
note.title: Definition of an Improper Integral of Type 1
note.heading: Definition of an Improper Integral of Type 1

list.item: (a) If $${\int_{a}^{t}{f(x)}}dx$$ exists for every number $$t \geqslant a$$ , then $${\int_{a}^{\infty}{f(x)}}dx = \lim\limits_{t\rightarrow\infty}{\int_{a}^{t}{f(x)}}dx$$ provided this limit exists (as a finite number).

(b) If $${\int_{t}^{b}{f(x)}}dx$$ exists for every number $$t \leqslant b$$ then $${\int_{- \infty}^{b}{f(x)}}dx = \lim\limits_{t\rightarrow - \infty}{\int_{t}^{b}{f(x)}}dx$$ provided this limit exists (as a finite number). The improper integrals $${\int_{a}^{\infty}{f(x)}}dx{and}{\int_{\infty}^{b}{f(x)}}dx$$ and are called convergent if the corresponding limit exists and divergent if the limit does not exist.

(c) If both $${\int_{a}^{\infty}{f(x)}}dx{and}{\int_{- \infty}^{a}{f(x)}}dx$$ are convergent, then we define $${\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}{f(x)}}dx = {\int_{- \infty}^{a}{f(x)}}dx + {\int_{a}^{\infty}{f(x)}}dx$$ In part (c) any real number $$a$$ can be used (see Exercise 88).

section.paragraph: Any of the improper integrals in Definition 1 can be interpreted as an area provided that $$f$$ is a positive function. For instance, in case (a) if $$f(x) \geqslant 0$$ and the integral $${\int_{a}^{\infty}{f(x)}}dx$$ is convergent, then we define the area of the region $$S = \left\{ {\left. \left( {x,y} \right) \right|x \geqslant a,0 \leqslant y \leqslant f(x)} \right\}$$ in Figure 3 to be
$$A(S) = {\int_{a}^{\infty}{f(x)}}dx$$
This is appropriate because $${\int_{a}^{\infty}{f(x)}}dx$$ is the limit as $$\left. t\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ of the area under the graph of $$f$$ from $$a$$ to $$t$$ .

image.alt: Details In the first quadrant of the x-y coordinate plane, a curve y = f(x) is graphed. The curve starts along the vertical axis, falls, rises gradually, reaches a peak, decreases gradually again rises reaches a peak, and then gradually goes down to the point where the curve is almost parallel to the x-axis. The starting point of the curve is connected with the point a along the horizontal axis.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Determine whether the integral $${\int_{1}^{\infty}\left( {1 \slash x} \right)}dx$$ is convergent or divergent.
Solution According to part (a) of Definition 1, we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {{{\int_{1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{x}}dx} = {\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow\infty}{\int_{1}^{t}\frac{1}{x}}dx = \left. {\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow\infty}\ln|x|} \right\rbrack_{1}^{t}}} \\ {\phantom{{\int_{1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{x}}dx} = {\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow\infty}\left( {\ln t - \ln 1} \right) = \lim\limits_{t\rightarrow\infty}\ln t = \infty}} \end{array}$$
The limit does not exist as a finite number and so the improper integral $${\int_{1}^{\infty}\left( {1 \slash x} \right)}dx$$ is divergent.

section.paragraph: Let’s compare the result of Example 1 with the example given at the beginning of this section:
$${{\int_{1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{x^{2}}}dx {converges}} {{\int_{1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{x}}dx {diverges}}$$

Geometrically, this says that although the curves $$y = 1 \slash x^{2}$$ and $$y = 1 \slash x$$ look very similar for $$x > 0$$ , the region under $$y = 1 \slash x^{2}$$ to the right of $$x = 1$$ (the shaded region in Figure 4) has finite area whereas the corresponding region under $$y = 1 \slash x$$ (in Figure 5) has infinite area. Note that both $$1 \slash x^{2}$$ and $$1 \slash x$$ approach $$0$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ but $$1 \slash x^{2}$$ approaches $$0$$ faster than $$1 \slash x$$ . The values of $$1 \slash x$$ don’t decrease fast enough for its integral to have a finite value.

The curve then rises at the point (1, 0) and goes up to the point where the curve is parallel to the y-axis. The points (1, 0) are connected with the curve. The area is shaded and the finite area is labeled on the right.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Evaluate $${\int_{- \infty}^{0}{xe^{ x}}}dx$$ .
Solution Using part (b) of Definition 1, we have
$${\int_{- \infty}^{0}{xe^{ x}}}dx = \lim\limits_{t\rightarrow - \infty}{\int_{t}^{0}{xe^{ x}}}dx$$
We integrate by parts with $$u = x$$ , $$d\upsilon = e^{ x}dx$$ so that $$du = dx$$ , $$\upsilon = e^{ x}$$ :
$$\begin{array}{l} {{{\int_{t}^{0}{xe^{ x}}}dx} = {\left. {xe^{ x}} \right\rbrack_{t}^{0} - {\int_{t}^{0}e^{ x}}dx}} \\ {\phantom{{\int_{t}^{0}{xe^{ x}}}dx} = {- te^{ t} - 1 + e^{ t}}} \end{array}$$
We know that $$\left. e^{ t}\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ as $$\left. t\rightarrow - \infty \right.$$ , and by l’Hospital’s Rule we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow - \infty}te^{ t}} = {\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow - \infty}\frac{t}{e^{- t}} = \lim\limits_{t\rightarrow - \infty}\frac{1}{- e^{- t}}}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow - \infty}te^{ t}} = {\underset{t\rightarrow - \infty}{\lim}{({- e^{ t}})} = 0}} \end{array}$$
Therefore

$$\begin{array}{l} {{{\int_{- \infty}^{0}{xe^{ x}}}dx} = {\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow - \infty}{({- te^{ t} - 1 + e^{ t}})}}} \\ {\phantom{{\int_{- \infty}^{0}{xe^{ x}}}dx} = {- 0 - 1 + 0 = - 1}} \end{array}$$

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Evaluate $${\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}\frac{1}{1 + x^{2}}}dx$$ .
Solution It’s convenient to choose $$a = 0$$ in Definition 1(c):
We must now evaluate the integrals on the right side separately:

$$\begin{array}{l} {{{\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{1 + x^{2}}}dx} = {\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow\infty}{\int_{0}^{t}\frac{dx}{1 + x^{2}}} = \lim\limits_{t\rightarrow\infty}\left. {\tan^{- 1}x} \right\rbrack_{0}^{t}}} \\ {\phantom{{\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{1 + x^{2}}}dx} = {\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow\infty}\left( {\tan^{- 1}t - \tan^{- 1}0} \right) = \lim\limits_{t\rightarrow\infty}\tan^{- 1}t = \frac{\pi}{2}}} \\ {{{\int_{- \infty}^{0}\frac{1}{1 + x^{2}}}dx} = {\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow - \infty}{\int_{t}^{0}\frac{dx}{1 + x^{2}}} = \lim\limits_{t\rightarrow - \infty}\left. {\tan^{- 1}x} \right\rbrack_{t}^{0}}} \\ {\phantom{{\int_{- \infty}^{0}\frac{1}{1 + x^{2}}}dx} = {\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow - \infty}\left( {\tan^{- 1}0 - \tan^{- 1}t} \right) = 0 - \left( {- \frac{\pi}{2}} \right) = \frac{\pi}{2}}} \end{array}$$
Since both of these integrals are convergent, the given integral is convergent and
$${\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}\frac{1}{1 + x^{2}}}dx = \frac{\pi}{2} + \frac{\pi}{2} = \pi$$

Since $$1 \slash \left( {1 + x^{2}} \right) > 0$$ , the given improper integral can be interpreted as the area of the infinite region that lies under the curve $$y = 1 \slash \left( {1 + x^{2}} \right)$$ and above the $$x$$ -axis (see Figure 6).

image.alt: Details A curve y=1/1+(x^2) is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The curve enters the second quadrant, which is parallel to the x-axis and gradually increases, reaches a peak along the y-axis, and then gradually decreases till it is parallel to the x-axis and exits through the first quadrant. The area=pi is shaded.

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: For what values of $$p$$ is the integral
$${\int_{1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{x^{p}}}dx$$
convergent?
Solution We know from Example 1 that if $$p = 1$$ , then the integral is divergent, so let’s assume that $$p \neq 1$$ . Then

$$\begin{array}{l} {{{\int_{1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{x^{p}}}dx} = {\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow\infty}{\int_{1}^{t}x^{- p}}dx = \lim\limits_{t\rightarrow\infty}\left. \frac{x^{- p + 1}}{- p + 1} \right\rbrack_{x = 1}^{x = t}}} \\ {\phantom{{\int_{1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{x^{p}}}dx} = {\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{1 - p}\left\lbrack {\frac{1}{t^{p - 1}} - 1} \right\rbrack}} \end{array}$$
If $$p > 1$$ , then $$p - 1 > 0$$ , so as $$\left. t\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ , $$\left. t^{p - 1}\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ and $$\left. 1 \slash t^{p - 1}\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ . Therefore
and so the integral converges.
If $$p < 1$$ , then $$p - 1 < 0$$ and so
$$\left. \frac{1}{t^{p - 1}} = t^{1 - p}\rightarrow\infty {as}t\rightarrow\infty \right.$$
and the integral diverges.

section.paragraph: We summarize the result of Example 4 for future reference:
$$\int_{1}^{\infty}{\frac{1}{x^{p}}dx{is}{convergent}{if}p > 1{and divergent if}p \leqslant 1.}$$
section.heading: Type 2: Discontinuous Integrands
section.paragraph: Suppose that $$f$$ is a positive continuous function defined on a finite interval $$\lbrack{a,b})$$ but has a vertical asymptote at $$b$$ . Let $$S$$ be the unbounded region under the graph of $$f$$ and above the $$x$$ -axis between $$a$$ and $$b$$ . (For Type 1 integrals, the regions extended indefinitely in a horizontal direction. Here the region is infinite in a vertical direction.) The area of the part of $$S$$ between $$a$$ and $$t$$ (the shaded region in Figure 7) is

image.alt: Details A sine wave is graphed in the first quadrant on the coordinate plane. The sine wave y=f(x) starts above the horizontal axis at the point (a, 0), and ends at the point (b, 0). The vertical line is extended from the point (t, 0) and ends with the wave. The area within this region is shaded. A vertical asymptote is drawn at (b, 0), labeled x=b.

section.paragraph: If it happens that $$A(t)$$ approaches a definite number $$A$$ as $$\left. t\rightarrow b^{-} \right.$$ , then we say that the area of the region $$S$$ is $$A$$ and we write
$${\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)}}dx = \lim\limits_{t\rightarrow b^{-}}{\int_{a}^{1}{f(x)}}dx$$
We use this equation to define an improper integral of Type 2 even when $$f$$ is not a positive function, no matter what type of discontinuity $$f$$ has at $$b$$ .

note.source_type: Definition of an Improper Integral of Type 2
note.title: Definition of an Improper Integral of Type 2
note.heading: Definition of an Improper Integral of Type 2

list.item: (a) If $$f$$ is continuous on $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right)$$ and is discontinuous at $$b$$ , then $${\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)}}dx = \lim\limits_{t\rightarrow b^{-}}{\int_{a}^{t}{f(x)}}dx$$ if this limit exists (as a finite number).

(b) If $$f$$ is continuous on $$\lbrack{a,b})$$ and is discontinuous at $$a$$ , then $${\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)}}dx = \lim\limits_{t\rightarrow a^{+}}{\int_{t}^{b}{f(x)}}dx$$ if this limit exists (as a finite number).

note.paragraph: The improper integral $${\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)}}dx$$ is called convergent if the corresponding limit exists and divergent if the limit does not exist.

list.item: (c) If $$f$$ has a discontinuity at $$c$$ , where $$a < c < b$$ , and both $${\int_{a}^{c}{f(x)}}dx$$ and $${\int_{c}^{b}{f(x)}}dx$$ are convergent, then we define $${\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)}}dx = {\int_{a}^{c}{f(x)}}dx + {\int_{c}^{b}{f(x)}}dx$$

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Find $${\int_{2}^{5}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x - 2}}}dx$$ .

Solution We note first that the given integral is improper because $$f(x) = 1 \slash \sqrt{x - 2}$$ has the vertical asymptote $$x = 2$$ . Since the infinite discontinuity occurs at the left endpoint of $$\left\lbrack {2,5} \right\rbrack$$ , we use part (b) of Definition 3:

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{2}^{5}\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x - 2}}} = {\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 2^{+}}{\int_{t}^{5}\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x - 2}}} = \lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 2^{+}}\left. {2\sqrt{x - 2}} \right\rbrack_{t}^{5}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{2}^{5}\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x - 2}}} = {\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 2^{+}}2\left( {\sqrt{3} - \sqrt{t - 2}} \right) = 2\sqrt{3}}} \end{array}$$
Thus the given improper integral is convergent and, since the integrand is positive, we can interpret the value of the integral as the area of the shaded region in Figure 10.

image.alt: Details A curve is graphed in the first quadrant on the coordinate plane. The concave downward curve y=1/sqrt (x negative 2) starts from a high point along the vertical axis and descends to the point where the curve is parallel to the horizontal axis. The vertical line is extended from the point (5, 0), and ends with the wave. A vertical asymptote is drawn at (2, 0). The area=2sqrt (3) is shaded.

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: Determine whether $${\int_{0}^{\pi \slash 2}{\sec x}}dx$$ converges or diverges.

Solution Note that the given integral is improper because $$\lim_{x\rightarrow{({\pi \slash 2})}^{-}}\sec x = \infty$$ . Using part (a) of Definition 3 and Formula 14 from the Table of Integrals, we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {{{\int_{0}^{\pi \slash 2}{\sec x}}dx} = {\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow{({\pi \slash 2})}^{-}}{\int_{0}^{t}{\sec x}}dx = \lim\limits_{t\rightarrow{({\pi \slash 2})}^{-}}\left. {\ln\left| {\sec x + \tan x} \right|} \right\rbrack_{0}^{t}}} \\ {\phantom{{\int_{0}^{\pi \slash 2}{\sec x}}dx} = {\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow{({\pi \slash 2})}^{-}}\left\lbrack {\ln\left( {\sec t + \tan t} \right) - \ln 1} \right\rbrack = \infty}} \end{array}$$

because $$\left. \sec t\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ and $$\left. \tan t\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ as $$\left. t\rightarrow\left( {\pi \slash 2} \right)^{-} \right.$$ . Thus the given improper integral is divergent.

example.heading: Example 7
example.paragraph: Evaluate $$\int_{0}^{3}\frac{dx}{x - 1}$$ if possible.

Solution Observe that the line $$x = 1$$ is a vertical asymptote of the integrand. Since it occurs in the middle of the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,3} \right\rbrack$$ , we must use part (c) of Definition 3 with $$c = 1$$ :
where

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{0}^{1}\frac{dx}{x - 1}} = {\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 1^{-}}{\int_{0}^{t}\frac{dx}{x - 1}} = \lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 1^{-}}\left. {\ln\left| {x - 1} \right|} \right\rbrack_{0}^{t}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{0}^{1}\frac{dx}{x - 1}} = {\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 1^{-}}\left( {\ln\left| {t - 1} \right| - \ln\left| {- 1} \right|} \right) = \lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 1^{-}}\ln\left( {1 - t} \right) = - \infty}} \end{array}$$

because $$\left. 1 - t\rightarrow 0^{+} \right.$$ as $$\left. t\rightarrow 1^{-} \right.$$ . Thus $$\int_{0}^{1}{dx \slash \left( {x - 1} \right)}$$ is divergent. This implies that $$\int_{0}^{3}{dx \slash \left( {x - 1} \right)}$$ is divergent. [We do not need to evaluate $$\int_{1}^{3}{dx \slash \left( {x - 1} \right)}$$ .]

section.paragraph: Warning If we had not noticed the asymptote $$x = 1$$ in Example 7 and had instead confused the integral with an ordinary integral, then we might have erroneously calculated $$\int_{0}^{3}{\mathit{dx}/(x - 1)}$$ as
$$\ln\left. \left| {x - 1} \right| \right\rbrack_{0}^{3} = \ln 2 - \ln 1 = \ln 2$$
This is wrong because the integral is improper and must be calculated in terms of limits.

From now on, whenever you see the symbol $${\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)}}dx$$ you must decide, by looking at the function $$f$$ on $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ , whether it is an ordinary definite integral or an improper integral.

example.heading: Example 8
example.paragraph: Evaluate $${\int_{0}^{1}{\ln x}}dx$$ .
Solution We know that the function $$f(x) = \ln x$$ has a vertical asymptote at $$0$$ because $$\lim_{x\rightarrow 0 +}\ln x = - \infty$$ . Thus the given integral is improper and we have
$${\int_{0}^{1}{\ln x}}dx = \lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 0^{+}}{\int_{t}^{1}{\ln x}}dx$$
Now we integrate by parts with $$u = \ln x$$ , $$d\upsilon = dx$$ , $$du = dx \slash x$$ , and $$\upsilon = x$$ :

$$\begin{array}{l} {{{\int_{t}^{1}{\ln x}}dx} = {\left. {x\ln x} \right\rbrack_{t}^{1} - {\int_{t}^{1}{dx}}}} \\ {\phantom{{\int_{t}^{1}{\ln x}}dx} = {1\ln 1 - t\ln t - \left( {1 - t} \right) = - t\ln t - 1 + t}} \end{array}$$
To find the limit of the first term we use l’Hospital’s Rule:

$$\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 0^{+}}t\ln t = \lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 0^{+}}\frac{\ln t}{1 \slash t} = \lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 0^{+}}\frac{1 \slash t}{- 1 \slash t^{2}} = \lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 0^{+}}\left( {- t} \right) = 0$$
Therefore
$${\int_{0}^{1}{\ln x}}dx = \lim\limits_{t\rightarrow 0^{+}}\left( {- t\ln t - 1 + t} \right) = - 0 - 1 + 0 = - 1$$
Figure 11 shows the geometric interpretation of this result. The area of the shaded region above $$y = \ln x$$ and below the $$x$$ -axis is $$1$$ .

It then descends to the fourth quadrant, and further to the point where the curve is almost parallel to the y-axis. The region labeled area=1 is shaded.

section.heading: A Comparison Test for Improper Integrals
section.paragraph: Sometimes it is impossible to find the exact value of an improper integral and yet it is important to know whether the integral is convergent or divergent. In such cases the following theorem is useful. Although we state it for Type 1 integrals, a similar theorem is true for Type 2 integrals.

note.title: Comparison Theorem
note.heading: Comparison Theorem
note.paragraph: Suppose that $$f$$ and $$g$$ are continuous functions with $$f(x) \geqslant g(x) \geqslant 0$$ for $$x \geqslant a$$ .

list.item: (a) If $${\int_{a}^{\infty}{f(x)}}dx$$ is convergent, then $${\int_{a}^{\infty}{g(x)}}dx$$ is convergent.
(b) If $${\int_{a}^{\infty}{g(x)}}dx$$ is divergent, then $${\int_{a}^{\infty}{f(x)}}dx$$ is divergent.

section.paragraph: We omit the proof of the Comparison Theorem, but Figure 12 makes it seem plausible. If the area under the top curve $$y = f(x)$$ is finite, then so is the area under the bottom curve $$y = g(x)$$ . And if the area under $$y = g(x)$$ is infinite, then so is the area under $$y = f(x)$$ . [Note that the reverse is not necessarily true: If $${\int_{a}^{\infty}{g(x)}}dx$$ is convergent, $${\int_{a}^{\infty}{f(x)}}dx$$ may or may not be convergent, and if $${\int_{a}^{\infty}{f(x)}}dx$$ is divergent, $${\int_{a}^{\infty}{g(x)}}dx$$ may or may not be divergent.]

image.alt: Details Two curves are graphed in the first quadrant on the x y coordinate plane. Curve 1: A vertical line is drawn at (a, 0) up to a high point. A concave downward curve f starts at the high point and gradually goes down to the point where the curve is almost parallel to the x-axis. Curve 2: The concave downward curve g starts at the midpoint of the vertical line, rises, reaches the peak, and gradually goes down to the point where the curve is almost parallel to the x-axis.

example.heading: Example 9
example.paragraph: Show that $${\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{- x^{2}}}dx$$ is convergent.
Solution
We can’t evaluate the integral directly because the antiderivative of $$e^{- x^{2}}$$ is not an elementary function (as explained in Section 7.5). We write

and observe that the first integral on the right-hand side is just an ordinary definite integral with a finite value. In the second integral we use the fact that for $$x \geqslant 1$$ we have $$x^{2} \geqslant x$$ , so $$- x^{2} \leqslant - x$$ and therefore $$e^{- x^{2}} \leqslant e^{- x}$$ . (See Figure 13.) The integral of $$e^{- x}$$ is easy to evaluate:
$${\int_{1}^{\infty}e^{- x}}dx = \lim\limits_{t\rightarrow\infty}{\int_{1}^{t}e^{- x}}dx = \lim\limits_{t\rightarrow\infty}{({e^{- 1} - e^{- t}})} = e^{- 1}$$

Therefore, taking $$f(x) = e^{- x}$$ and $$g(x) = e^{- x^{2}}$$ in the Comparison Theorem, we see that $${\int_{1}^{\infty}e^{- x^{2}}}dx$$ is convergent. It follows that $${\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{- x^{2}}}dx$$ is convergent also.

image.alt: Details Two curves are graphed in the first quadrant on the x y coordinate plane. Curve 1: A concave downward curve y=e^ (negative x) starts at the high point along the vertical axis and gradually goes down to the point where the curve is almost parallel to the x-axis. Curve 2: The curve y=e^ (negative x^2) starts at the high point along the vertical axis, rises, and gradually decreases to the point where the curve is almost parallel to the x-axis. The curves are intersected at the point (1, 0).

section.paragraph: In Example 9 we showed that $${\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{- x^{2}}}dx$$ is convergent without computing its value. In Exercise 84 we indicate how to show that its value is approximately $$0.8862$$ . In probability theory it is important to know the exact value of this improper integral, as we will see in Section 8.5; using the methods of multivariable calculus it can be shown that the exact value is $$\sqrt{\pi} \slash 2$$ . Table 1 illustrates the definition of a convergent improper integral by showing how the (computer-generated) values of $${\int_{0}^{t}e^{- x^{2}}}dx$$ approach $$\sqrt{\pi} \slash 2$$ as $$t$$ becomes large. In fact, these values converge quite quickly because $$\left. e^{- x^{2}}\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ very rapidly as $$\left. x\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ .

section.heading: Table 2
